torque-work-s2.title: A motor spinning up a wheel
torque-work-s2.text: A motor exerts a torque on a wheel (I = 0.50 kg·m²) on a frictionless axle. The graph shows the torque against the angle the wheel has turned since it started from rest.

items.q: What torque does the rope exert on the drum while the bucket rises at constant speed?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides the force by the radius. τ = rF.
Value: that uses the mass instead of the rope’s force. At constant speed the tension is mg.

why.correct: At constant speed the rope’s tension equals the bucket’s weight, (6.00 kg)(9.8 m/s²) = 58.8 N. The rope pulls tangent to the drum, so τ = rF = (0.0800 m)(58.8 N) = 4.70 N·m.

items.q: How much work does the crank do on the drum while it turns through 25.0 rad? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that divides by 2π, as if the 25.0 rad were degrees or revolutions. W = τΔθ with Δθ in radians.
Value: that converts 25.0 rad to degrees. W = τΔθ needs radians.

why.correct: W = τΔθ = (4.704 N·m)(25.0 rad) = 117.6 J, about 118 J. (No friction and constant speed, so the crank’s torque equals the rope’s.)

items.q: How far does the bucket rise?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides the angle by r. The rope wound up is s = rθ.
Value: that treats 25.0 rad as 25.0 revolutions. s = rθ with θ in radians.

why.correct: The rope winds onto the drum without slipping: s = rθ = (0.0800 m)(25.0 rad) = 2.00 m.

items.q: How does the work done by the torque on the drum compare with the increase in the bucket’s gravitational potential energy?
options: They are equal: nothing speeds up and there is no friction
The work is larger, because some goes into spinning the drum
The work is smaller, because the drum’s radius is small
The work is a rotational quantity, so it is not an energy

why.correct: For the drum-rope-bucket system, the crank’s work all goes into gravitational potential energy: τΔθ = (r · mg)(θ) = mg(rθ) = mgΔy = 117.6 J. Nothing speeds up and there is no friction.
options: Right: τΔθ = (rmg)θ = mg(rθ) = mgΔy.
The drum turns at a steady rate, so its kinetic energy does not change.
A small radius means a small torque but a large angle; the product is the same.
Both are energies in joules; τΔθ = mgΔy here.

items.q: How much work does the motor do on the wheel from 0 to 8.0 rad?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides torque by angle. Work is the area under the τ-θ graph: τΔθ.

why.correct: Constant torque: W = τΔθ = (6.0 N·m)(8.0 rad) = 48 J, the rectangle under the graph.

items.q: How much work does the motor do on the wheel from 0 to 14.0 rad?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses 6.0 N·m for the whole 14.0 rad. From 8.0 to 14.0 rad the torque falls to zero: take the triangle’s area.
Value: that stops at 8.0 rad. Add the triangle from 8.0 to 14.0 rad.

why.correct: Area under the graph: (6.0 N·m)(8.0 rad) + ½(6.0 N·m)(6.0 rad) = 48 + 18 = 66 J.

items.q: The wheel (I = 0.50 kg·m²) starts from rest on a frictionless axle. How fast is it turning at 14.0 rad?

mistakes.why: Value: that is ω². Take the square root.
Value: the ½ was dropped. W = ½Iω², so ω = √(2W/I).

why.correct: The net work equals the change in rotational kinetic energy: 66 J = ½(0.50 kg·m²)ω², so ω = √(2 × 66/0.50) = √264 = 16.2 rad/s, about 16 rad/s.

items.q: Between 8.0 rad and 14.0 rad, the wheel
options: keeps speeding up, more and more gently
slows down, because the torque is decreasing
turns at a constant angular velocity
speeds up more and more quickly

why.correct: The net torque is positive (in the direction of turning) until 14.0 rad, so the wheel keeps gaining kinetic energy, but the torque and so α = τ/I shrink to zero.
options: Right: the torque is still positive but shrinking, so α > 0 and falling.
A smaller positive torque still speeds the wheel up; it does not slow it.
That would need zero net torque; the torque is positive until 14.0 rad.
The torque, and so α, is decreasing.

items.q: The work done on a wheel by a constant torque τ while it turns through an angle Δθ is
options: τΔθ, with Δθ in radians
τΔθ, with Δθ in degrees
τ/Δθ
½τΔθ²

why.correct: W = τΔθ, the partner of W = Fd. The angle must be in radians, the same reason s = rθ needs radians.
options: Right: the rotational version of W = Fd.
W = τΔθ only works in radians.
Work is torque times angle, not torque per angle.
There is no ½ or square for a constant torque.

items.q: A screwdriver applies a constant torque of 1.5 N·m while turning a screw through 4 full revolutions. How much work is done?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses 4 as the angle. Convert revolutions to radians: 4 × 2π rad.
Value: that uses degrees. W = τΔθ needs radians.

why.correct: Δθ = 4 × 2π rad = 25.1 rad, so W = τΔθ = (1.5 N·m)(25.1 rad) = 37.7 J, about 38 J.

items.q: A wheel turns counterclockwise. A brake exerts a clockwise torque on it. The work done by the brake’s torque is
options: negative, and the wheel loses kinetic energy
positive, because the torque is not zero
zero, because a brake does not move
negative, and the wheel gains kinetic energy

why.correct: W = τΔθ with signs: the torque (clockwise, −) and the angular displacement (counterclockwise, +) have opposite signs, so W < 0 and the wheel’s rotational kinetic energy falls.
options: Right: the torque opposes the turning, so it takes energy out.
Work by a torque is positive only when the torque is in the direction of turning.
The wheel turns through an angle while the torque acts, so work is done on it.
Negative work removes kinetic energy.

items.q: A wheel with I = 2.0 kg·m² spins at 15 rad/s. A brake stops it while the wheel turns through 30 rad. What constant braking torque does this take?

mistakes.why: Value: ω was not squared in ½Iω².
Value: the ½ in ½Iω² was dropped.

why.correct: The brake removes all the kinetic energy: ½Iω² = ½(2.0 kg·m²)(15 rad/s)² = 225 J = τ(30 rad), so τ = 7.5 N·m.

items.q: On a graph of torque against angle for a wheel, what does the area under the line represent?
options: The work done on the wheel
The wheel’s angular velocity
The wheel’s angular acceleration
The wheel’s rotational inertia

why.correct: Area under τ-θ is τΔθ summed over the angle, the work done by the torque (in J), just as the area under F-x is the work done by a force.
options: Right: area = τ × Δθ, in joules.
Angular velocity comes from an ω-t or θ-t graph, not τ-θ.
α is the net torque divided by I, not an area on this graph.
I is a property of the wheel, not an area on this graph.

items.q: A motor applies the same constant torque to two wheels, starting from rest, through the same angle. Wheel 2 has twice the rotational inertia of wheel 1. Compared with wheel 1, wheel 2 ends with
options: the same kinetic energy and a smaller angular velocity
half the kinetic energy and the same angular velocity
the same kinetic energy and the same angular velocity
twice the kinetic energy and the same angular velocity

why.correct: Each gains K = τΔθ, the same. Then ½(2I)ω₂² = ½Iω₁², so ω₂ = ω₁/√2, about 0.71 times as large.
options: Right: same work, so same K; K = ½Iω² with larger I means smaller ω.
The work, τΔθ, is the same for both, so they gain the same energy.
The same K with twice the I needs a smaller ω.
The work is the same, so the energy gained is the same.

items.q: A constant torque spins up a wheel from rest on a frictionless axle. Predict how each quantity changes as the wheel turns through more and more angle.

variables.name: Work done on the wheel so far
variables.why: W = τΔθ grows with the angle turned.

variables.name: The wheel’s rotational kinetic energy
variables.why: With no friction, all the work becomes rotational kinetic energy.

variables.name: The wheel’s rotational inertia
variables.why: I depends on the wheel’s mass and its distribution, which do not change.

why.correct: The work done by the torque, τΔθ, grows with the angle and all of it becomes rotational kinetic energy; the wheel itself, and so its I, is unchanged.
